A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
, for any key length, there exists a network that sorts n k -bit integers in O(log n loglog n ) time and area, and a sorting network for n k -bit inputs with area O(n log n loglog n ).
the area-time complexity for short keys is O(n log n log n), and for long keys, O(n log n).
for short keys the area-time tradeoff is the same as for sorting n numbers and for long keys the area-time product is proportional to the key length.
The main takeaway from our work is that
for sorting, key length is a critical design parameter and that short keys are much easier to sort than long keys.
, for short keys, a simple network based on a sorting network of the same size is optimal; for long keys, a network based on a tree is optimal.
the area-time complexity is not a function of the key size alone; it also depends on the number of keys to be sorted, the number of keys per chip, and whether the keys are short or long.
